title: My First film
purpose:
Many Uzbek students work hard to achieve their goals, yet their daily struggles are often misunderstood. Parents, teachers, and society frequently compare today's generation to their own, assuming young people are lazy or unmotivated without fully understanding the pressures they face.
I believe documentary filmmaking—an underdeveloped genre in Uzbekistan—can help change this. By following the everyday lives of real students from different backgrounds, we want to tell authentic stories that reveal their challenges, dreams, resilience, humor, and growth. Rather than telling audiences what to think, we want them to experience these stories firsthand and form their own perspectives.
Our primary audience is parents, teachers, and school psychologists, while our secondary audience is teenagers who feel misunderstood or lack motivation. Unlike traditional documentaries, our films blend cinematic storytelling, humor, and emotional moments to create engaging stories people want to watch, building empathy and showing the untapped potential of documentary filmmaking in Uzbekistan.

title: Uzbek Television Drama and Regional Soft Power: A Comparative Analysis with the Korean and Turkish Models
description: Television drama has become one of the most effective instruments of national soft power in the twenty-first century, as demonstrated by South Korea's globally distributed Hallyu and Turkey's soap-opera exports across the Middle East and Balkans. This study asks how the current content pattern of Uzbek television dramas shapes both domestic public discourse and Uzbekistan's cultural image abroad, compared to the Korean and Turkish models. Drawing on a review of seven academic sources spanning soft power theory, Korean and Turkish case studies, and existing Uzbek media scholarship, this study applies a qualitative content and discourse analysis to a purposive sample of Uzbek television dramas, comparing production patterns, thematic content, and audience and institutional reception against the Korean and Turkish cases. The findings indicate that Uzbekistan's industry remains overwhelmingly commercial and concentrated in domestic/family-conflict narratives, with a single state-initiated exception offering a viable template for future development, while its already-engaged domestic audience represents an underused asset for improving both content quality and international cultural reach.
